78: Our base is a permitted commissary, and we do not build one. A paella caterer cannot legally prep for clients at home, so we rent time in a shared commissary kitchen that already holds the health permit. That is where the sofrito, the stock and the cleaned seafood are made the day before, where the cold and dry storage lives, and where the pans and burners sleep between events. Ask every commissary one question before you sign: does it allow propane cylinders on the property? The example budgets {{alquiler_mes}} per month for all of it. Published rates for shared kitchens typically run from $15 to $45 an hour depending on the city and the equipment, according to The Food Corridor, so we compare at least three commissaries on price, on hours that fit a Saturday-heavy schedule, on cooler space and on how early we can load on event days. Before paying a deposit we sign a written commissary agreement that spells out our hours, our shelves and refrigeration, where the gear is stored, cleaning duties, insurance requirements and notice for ending the arrangement. The rule we keep is simple: own what travels with you and rent what you use a few days a week. The only things that happen in front of the guests are the ones worth watching, and everything else arrives measured and ready.
79: The equipment list follows the order in which the food moves, so we buy in that order too. First, what cooks: the paella burners and stands ({{inv_quemadores}}), the pans ({{inv_paelleras}}) and the propane and fire-safety kit ({{inv_propano}}). Size each pan by how many guests it feeds: as a Kit estimate, a 36 in (90 cm) pan serves about 40 guests, a 32 in (80 cm) pan about 30 and a 26 in (65 cm) pan about 18. Second, what protects: the canopy over the cooking station, the extinguishers and the fire blanket. Third, what holds and serves: tables, a handwashing station, coolers, chafing dishes and insulated carriers, all in the event setup and holding line ({{inv_montaje}}). The used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}) and its upfit with upright racks for the cylinders ({{inv_furgoneta_upfit}}) come with the plan, so nothing in it depends on a vehicle you may already own.
80: Every event follows the same phases, from the quote to the final payment. About three weeks out we hold the briefing with the client to confirm the menu style, the guest count, the timeline and the allergies. About two weeks out we visit the venue to choose where the cooking station goes, away from the guest tent, and to check water, power and van access. One to two days ahead we order the seafood and keep its tags. The day before, in the commissary, we make the sofrito and the stock and clean the seafood, and we label everything. On the day we arrive two to three hours early, set up the cooking station, light the burners and cook for about an hour; service runs about two hours and breakdown about one, according to Miami Grill Catering's published timeline. Plan one team member for every 25 guests. Afterward we clean and oil the pans, close the cylinders and send the final invoice with any add-ons. Write the times down for every event: that log is your best defense if a guest ever complains.
81: Cooked rice is a time and temperature control for safety food, and the FDA Food Code, in its Annex 3, notes that Bacillus cereus is found commonly in outbreaks tied to poor hot holding of starchy foods like rice. So we serve paella at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, or hold it under a written time as a public health control procedure for up to 4 hours, and leftovers go in the trash, never back into the pan. Quality and safety are different things: the socarrat is a taste target, while the Food Code minimums are 165 °F (74 °C) for chicken, 145 °F (63 °C) for 15 seconds for fish and shellfish and 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds for raw Mexican-style chorizo; cured Spanish chorizo is ready to eat. Raw seafood travels in coolers at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. Declare the allergens on every quote: crustacean shellfish and fish are among the nine major U.S. allergens, and we list mollusks too, along with the egg in the aioli and the sulfites in frozen shrimp.
82: We buy seafood only from an approved source, and we keep the invoices and the tags that come on mussels and clams. Chicken and vegetables come from a restaurant supplier or a cash-and-carry such as Restaurant Depot, whichever gives the better price and the steadier quality. Bomba rice and saffron come from an importer of Spanish foods, and we always keep a backup supplier for each item. Propane comes from a refill or exchange service, and a party rental company covers the tables, linens and any chafing dishes we do not own. Keep a maintenance calendar for the van and a small stock of spares: burner parts, hoses, regulators and a replacement pan, because a gas fitting that fails on a Saturday costs more than the part.
85: The team is small and every role has a clear job. The owner is the paella chef, who also sells, buys and cooks at the events that matter most. A lead cook, who doubles as the second paella chef, is a part-time hourly W-2 employee who runs the second pan line and covers the big events. Event staff, meaning servers and buffet attendants, are hourly W-2 employees who work event by event, and a prep cook who doubles as the van driver works part time. There is no dining room, no front-of-house manager and no office, so the payroll flexes with the calendar and the events pay for the structure.
86: Labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, which is {{personal_pct}} of sales. That figure includes the owner's pay and the employer payroll taxes for everyone on the payroll. It is the biggest line after the food, and it moves with the calendar: in a May with three weddings and two graduations everyone works, and in February almost nobody does. The owner's pay and the second paella chef's pay are fixed, while event staff cost depends on the hours of each event. If you book fewer events than planned, you schedule fewer hours and the cost drops; if you book more, you carry them with the same people until the coverage runs out and then add someone to the payroll, never a contractor who invoices you by the event. Change the "Staffing" sheet to your own wage rates before you show this plan to a lender.
87: Every event takes hours of prep, loading, travel, setup, cooking, service and breakdown. The workbook assumes {{horas_evento}} hours per person and {{personas_evento}} people per event on average, and it compares the hours scheduled with the hours needed to give a coverage of {{cobertura_horas}}. As a rule of thumb, plan one team member for every 25 guests, according to Miami Grill Catering. One paella chef can run about three pans at once, and a Kit estimate is to add a helper from four pans or about 80 guests. High coverage does not mean you have too many people. It means the roster can carry the busy Saturdays, including a weekend with two weddings. The workbook spreads payroll evenly over the 12 months, which is conservative.
88: Everyone but the owner is a W-2 employee. Event staff work under our direction, on our schedule and with our equipment, which is the profile the Fair Labor Standards Act treats as employment, and California's AB5 presumes it. Calling them contractors may look cheaper, but misclassification can bring back taxes, penalties and claims, and it can sink a loan application. Payroll taxes add {{cargas_pct}} to wages in the model, workers' compensation is required in nearly every state (Texas is the exception: coverage is optional there, but venues and lenders often ask for it), and you pay at least the highest of the federal, state and local minimum wage; the workbook uses the federal floor of {{salario_minimo_federal}} for full-time work as its reference, and many states are higher. For wages, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (OEWS, May 2025) puts restaurant cooks at a mean of $18.62 an hour, with the 75th percentile at $21.45, and food servers outside restaurants at $17.37, with the 75th percentile at $18.51. Check your city before you set rates.
89: Training is part of the plan, not an extra. The owner or the lead cook holds a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe Manager, and every employee who handles food gets the food handler card that your state or county requires. Training covers raw seafood, rice temperatures, time as a public health control and the nine major allergens, because a guest with an allergy has to be able to ask the person at the pan and get the right answer. Add fire and propane safety: where the extinguisher and the fire blanket are, how to shut off a cylinder and how far the canopy sits from the burners. Before the first event of the season, the crew rehearses the script for the live paella: when the burners are lit, when the stock goes in, how the socarrat is explained and when it is revealed. The rehearsal costs a morning and saves you from improvising in front of a hundred guests.
90: Handle the service charge and the gratuity differently, because the IRS does. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge that the client must pay is treated as wages to the staff who receive it, so payroll taxes apply. A gratuity is voluntary, the amount is the guest's choice and it belongs to the staff. We list them on separate lines of the quote, say plainly what each one pays for and distribute gratuities under a written policy. Check your state's overtime rules too, because a wedding that ends late after an early start is a long shift. Whether the service charge is subject to sales tax depends on your state, which the legal section covers.
93: Taken together, the case describes a small business that is viable on paper. Year-1 sales are {{ventas_a1}}, the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}} and EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. The average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. These are planning figures from the workbook, not a forecast: they hold as long as you book the events in the plan at the average price of the mix. That average includes the corporate drop-offs and the backyard parties, which sell for less, so it is not the price of a wedding. The listings we read agree with the range: live paella with salad and bread from $12 to $31 per person, and full Spanish menus with staff from $44 to $65. The next sections show where each number comes from.
94: The investment is built from lines you can price today. The largest are the used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}) and the paella pans ({{inv_paelleras}}), followed by the burners and stands ({{inv_quemadores}}), the van upfit ({{inv_furgoneta_upfit}}), the event setup and holding gear ({{inv_montaje}}) and the propane and fire-safety kit ({{inv_propano}}). Then come the website, photos and first bridal show ({{inv_lanzamiento}}), first-year permits and certifications ({{inv_permisos}}) and the opening inventory ({{inv_stock}}). Startup costs also include a 10% contingency on the burners, the pans, the van and its upfit and the fire inspection, and they add up to {{capex}}. On top we set aside working capital of {{fondo_maniobra}}, which covers the first months while payments come in, for a total investment of {{inversion_total}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. A loan of that size means a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, not a Microloan. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is not guaranteed: the terms are an illustration, not an offer, so get quotes for the van and the pans before you treat any figure as closed.
95: Revenue grows with the number of events, not with the price. The workbook raises events by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{eventos_a1}} to {{eventos_a2}} and then {{eventos_a3}}, at the same price per guest and the same guests per event. That takes sales from {{ventas_a1}} in year 1 to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3, and net profit from {{resultado_neto_a1}} to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. Growth in events is realistic only if repeat business builds: companies that reorder, venues that send you bookings and families that return for the next birthday. The model applies an income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}} as a reserve; with a pass-through LLC the owner pays that tax on a personal return, so keeping the reserve is the prudent choice. Capacity matters too, because one crew and one set of pans can only cover so many Saturdays.
96: The cost structure can be checked against reference ranges. Food cost on paella package sales is {{coste_paquetes_pct}}, and all goods together are {{cogs_pct}} of sales. Disposables and cooking fuel add {{consumibles_pct}}, mostly propane, because it grows with the number of events you cook. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales, and the commissary and equipment storage are {{ocupacion_pct}}, or {{ocupacion_anual}} a year. Marketing is {{marketing_anual}} a year, insurance is {{seguros_anual}} and year-1 interest is {{intereses_a1}}. For reference, catering food cost typically runs from 28% to 35% of sales according to Galley Solutions, and net margins from 7% to 8% according to ItsaCheckmate. If your food cost sits above that range, check your portions and your seafood prices first.
97: Break-even is measured in events per year. On an accounting basis the business covers its costs with {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. On a cash basis, with loan payments in and depreciation out, it needs {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}}, against {{eventos_a1}} in the plan. That leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even: events can fall {{caida_absorbible_pct}} before cash stops covering costs. It is a real cushion, but not a wide one, and a slow spring can eat it. The workbook shows the exact figure and the plan rounds up to whole events. Track it every month.
98: You can fail on cash even when the profit looks good. The workbook assumes you collect from clients in {{cobro_dias}} days on average and pay suppliers in {{pago_dias}} days, with payroll going out every month. The lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, the lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}} and the payback before debt is {{payback}}. A deposit of 25% to 50% is common among U.S. caterers (Kit estimate), and the pricing calculator proposes 50%, but the workbook does not model it, so real cash should be a little better than the workbook shows.
99: Two scenarios show how fast the numbers move. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_eventos}} events at {{pesimista_invitados}} guests and {{pesimista_precio}} per guest, which gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. Year-1 closing cash comes out at {{pesimista_caja}}: the cash runs out, and you would need more equity, a credit line or lower spending before you get there. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_ventas}} with {{optimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. Remember that {{eventos_a1}} events is the pace of a full-time paella chef with a second cook, not the average first year. With a thin cushion you have four levers: book more corporate events, adjust the price, add guests per event and negotiate more time with your lender. The workbook rules: if you change a green cell, this document falls behind.
102: You cannot run a paella catering business from your home kitchen. The FDA Food Code (section 3-201.11) requires food to come from sources that comply with the law and says that food prepared in a private home may not be used. Cottage food laws do not rescue you either: paella with seafood, chicken or cooked rice needs time and temperature control, and those laws are written for low-risk foods, so check your state rules. That is why this plan preps in a permitted commissary and signs a written commissary agreement, and why that agreement comes before your health permit. This section is general information, not legal advice.
103: With the kitchen secured, the next layer is the local health permit. Expect to apply to your county for a catering or food facility permit, pay an annual fee and pass an inspection of the commissary. At least one person should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe Manager, and food handlers need the card your state requires. Your written food safety plan is based on HACCP principles and the FDA Food Code, and the rice is its center: cooked rice is a time and temperature control food, and Bacillus cereus is a known risk when it is held warm. Serve at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, or use time as a public health control for up to 4 hours with a written procedure and a marked start time, if your county allows it; whatever is left at the end goes in the trash. Cook chicken to 165 °F (74 °C) and fish and shellfish to 145 °F (63 °C). Buy only from an approved source and keep shellstock tags for 90 days (section 3-203.12). The nine major allergens include fish and crustacean shellfish such as crab, lobster or shrimp.
104: The permit question gets harder when the paella is cooked at the event. The Food Code counts a catering operation as a food establishment (section 1-201.10), and counties handle it differently. San Diego County is one example: food is prepared in the commissary, and limited food preparation is allowed at private catered events with a predetermined guest list, schedule and quantities, with a 5-gallon handwashing setup, restrooms nearby, a barrier or rope between the fire and the public, no cooking from a vehicle, logs kept 90 days and leftovers discarded. Other counties may say no. So ask your county whether cooking the rice on site fits its rule, and which permit that takes. If it does not, cook in the commissary and bring the paella in hot, in insulated carriers. A public event open to everyone is a different thing, a temporary food establishment, and this plan does not cover it.
105: Fire rules decide where a burner can run. As an example, Virginia's fire code says cooking tents must stand at least 20 feet (6 m) from other tents and keeps LP-gas containers outside the tent. Your city or county may be stricter or silent, so check with your fire marshal before you sign anything. The rule this plan follows is simple: the cooking station sits outdoors or under its own canopy, well away from the guest tent, with an extinguisher within reach and whatever permit the local fire code asks for. A wood-fire setup is only a bonus, and only where a permit allows it and no burn ban applies; for indoor venues, plan on induction. The contract has a plan B for wind, rain or a fire marshal who says no: move the cooking station, switch to induction or cook in the commissary and serve hot.
106: Sales tax is where small caterers get surprised. In many states it applies to the whole catering invoice, including food, staff and rentals, and the treatment of a service charge depends on the state: California taxes a mandatory one, and Texas excludes it up to 20% when it is separately stated and paid to qualified employees. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge is wages, not a tip. Register for a sales tax permit in your state; the workbook applies {{sales_tax}} to the whole invoice, which is the conservative choice. Sangria needs a decision, because without a license you cannot sell alcohol. Offer it without alcohol as an add-on, or make it with wine the client buys, with no markup and no paid bar.
107: Hiring and insurance come next. Event staff, the second paella chef and the prep cook belong on W-2 payroll with workers' compensation (optional only in Texas, where venues and lenders still ask for it), Form I-9, Form W-4 and your state's new-hire reporting. The FLSA treats servers as employees in almost every case, and California's AB5 presumes it, so a 1099 is a risk. The example budgets {{seguros_anual}} a year for general liability or a business owner's policy, commercial auto that covers the van, workers' compensation and inland marine for the pans, burners and equipment in transit. Ask in writing that the general liability policy does not exclude open flame at events. Insureon publishes average prices by policy, so get quotes from an agent who knows caterers, and ask venues for the certificate of insurance and additional insured wording they require before you quote.
108: The last link is the road. The van is titled and registered with your state DMV in the business name, and your auto policy has to cover commercial use. Federal rules require a commercial driver's license only at a vehicle rating of 26,001 lb or more, which a cargo van does not reach. Carry the cylinders upright, secured and with ventilation. If you operate in the UK, the rules differ: register your food business with the local council at least 28 days before you start trading, expect a Food Hygiene Rating from 0 to 5 (the FHIS in Scotland), keep a HACCP-based plan, declare the 14 listed allergens, which add mollusks, celery and sulphites to the U.S. nine, charge VAT at 20% on event catering once you are VAT-registered, and agree the gas and the fire plan with the council and the venue.
111: The plan holds up because of how it is built. There is no restaurant to lease or fit out: the paella chef preps in a shared, permitted commissary, and the cargo van carries the gear to the event, where the cooking is the product. Two engines of demand share the calendar, private celebrations and companies that reorder. The case is viable: sales of {{ventas_a1}}, net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a lowest DSCR of {{dscr_min}} and a payback of {{payback}}. But be honest about the margin. The cushion over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}, a pace of {{eventos_a1}} events is a full-time operator's, and in the pessimistic case the cash runs out. If volume stalls, you have the levers: more corporate events, price, guests per event and more time with your lender.
112: Know the risks before you sign anything. A late cancellation is handled with the deposit and a cancellation schedule in the contract. Wind, rain or an open flame the fire marshal does not allow are handled with a canopy over the cooking station, induction for indoor venues, cooking in the commissary and serving hot, or a new date. Rice out of temperature is the risk that can hurt a guest: it is prevented by holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above or under a written time as a public health control procedure, by throwing leftovers away and by liability insurance. A jump in seafood prices is handled by reviewing the pricing calculator with your own costs every season. A propane incident is prevented with leak tests, secured cylinders and extinguishers. A shortage of staff on peak Saturdays is handled with a bench of trained part-time hourly W-2 employees. Inspections hold no surprises if your permits, logs and commissary agreement are in order.
113: Our strengths come from the show. We sell a short list of things and do them in front of the guests, with a paella chef who explains the sofrito, the stock and the socarrat. Eight menu styles let us fit a wedding, a company or a birthday without reinventing the business, from seafood paella to farm vegetable. Our price includes the paella chef and the staff, which many competitors charge separately. A permitted commissary and written allergen handling give planners and venues the reassurance they look for. Fixed costs stay low because we share the commissary and run one van, so a slow month hurts less. And our best sales argument is not price. It is the memory of a paella cooked in front of you.
114: The roadmap follows the six phases of the startup checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" covers the LLC, the tax registrations, the bank account, the loan application and your contract. "Phase 2 - Propane & Permits" covers the commissary agreement, the health permit, the fire marshal and the propane setup, the van and the insurance. "Phase 3 - Equipment" covers the burners, the pans, the event gear, the suppliers and a full test cook. "Phase 4 - Staff" covers W-2 hiring, payroll and training. "Phase 5 - Marketing" builds the website, the Google Business Profile, the directory listings, the venue and planner outreach and the first tastings. "Phase 6 - First 90 Days" runs the first events and reviews each one against the plan. The phases overlap week by week, but do not book a paid event while any permit is still open.
115: Measure a few things every week and do not wait for your accountant. Track events booked per month and the share of quotes that become signed contracts. Compare your average price per guest, excluding sales tax, with the {{precio_invitado}} in the plan, remembering that it is an average of the mix and drops with the backyard parties. Track the ounces of rice per guest and the real number of guests each pan serves, your food cost against the {{cogs_pct}} in the plan, the propane used per event and the labor hours per event against the workbook. Log cancellations, events where a burn ban or rain changed the plan, and the reviews you collect. Each month, compare your cash balance with the lowest balance in the workbook, {{saldo_minimo}}. If three weeks go by without a signed event, do not wait for the end of the quarter: review your price, your outreach and your calendar.
116: Over three years, the plan is to build a base of clients who come back: weddings by referral, companies that reorder and venues that recommend us. That smooths the calendar and lowers the sales cost of every event, while events grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3. Sales reach {{ventas_a3}} and net profit {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3. A second paella chef full time, or a second cooking line with another van, makes sense only when the peak-season calendar is full and you are turning down dates, not before. A restaurant of your own is a different business with different numbers, and it makes sense only if your results ask for it. Meanwhile, growth comes from filling the events you already have more profitably: a higher guest count, better add-ons such as a tapas hour, and more repeat bookings.
117: The next steps are simple, and they go in order. Open the Excel workbook and replace the example figures with yours in the green cells: events per year, price per guest and guests per event. If you change one of them, this document falls behind, so the workbook rules. Use the pricing calculator, with its "Paella Yield & Pan Sizing" and its "Shopping List by Guest Count", to turn your costs into quotes you can send, and use the checklist so no permit gets skipped. This plan is a planning tool, not legal or tax advice: confirm what applies to you with your accountant, your county health department and your fire marshal. And keep an eye on years 2 and 3, when the loan is being repaid and the cushion over cash break-even matters most.
